abstract.p: Neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC), neuroendocrine tumor grade 3 (NET G3), and pancreatic cancer (PC) are aggressive malignancies with limited effective treatments. This study assessed the efficacy and safety of surufatinib combined with the PD-1 inhibitor sintilimab, with or without chemotherapy. In this phase II trial, 51 patients with advanced NEC (n = 30), NET G3 (n = 12), or PC (n = 9) received surufatinib plus sintilimab; the NEC cohort additionally received chemotherapy. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR), disease control rate (DCR), overall survival (OS), and safety. As of August 31, 2025, the median follow-up was 18.6 months. In the NEC cohort, median PFS was 7.3 months, median OS was 13.3 months, and ORR was 53.3%. First-line NEC patients achieved superior outcomes (mPFS 7.6 months; mOS 14.3 months; ORR 65.0%) versus later-line therapy. Median PFS was 6.8 months in the NET G3 cohort and 2.1 months in the PC cohort. Adverse events were manageable; no treatment-related death occurred. Surufatinib plus sintilimab with or without chemotherapy shows encouraging efficacy and acceptable safety in advanced NEC, NET G3, and PC. This clinical trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05627427) on November 15, 2022.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs) represent a collection of highly heterogeneous malignant tumors that can arise in various organs throughout the body, and their incidence has been increasing globally1,2 According to the degree of differentiation and the proliferation index (Ki-67), NENs are categorized into well-differentiated, biologically relatively indolent neuroendocrine tumor (NET) and poorly differentiated, highly aggressive neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC)3,4 High-grade NENs comprise both NET grade 3 (NET G3) and NEC, which demonstrate substantial differences in clinical behavior, management approaches, and outcomes. Accurate differentiation between NET G3 and NEC is crucial. According to the 2022 WHO classification5, NET G3 is well-differentiated with preserved organoid architecture, shows positive expression of SSTR and Rb, and typically exhibits wild-type P53. In contrast, NEC is poorly differentiated with a disorganized structure, often shows loss of SSTR and Rb expression, and frequently demonstrates aberrant P53 expression. NET G3 tends to grow more slowly and is often positive on SSTR-PET imaging, whereas NEC is highly aggressive and typically shows high uptake on FDG-PET. While first-line chemotherapy with etoposide paired with cisplatin (EP) or carboplatin (EC) is the standard regimen for advanced NEC, its effectiveness is constrained, and most patients experience disease progression within a brief timeframe. Therapeutic alternatives for second line and subsequent treatments are notably scarce, and the median overall survival (OS) is merely ~10 months, representing a considerable challenge in clinical oncology practice6–9.

Pancreatic cancer (PC) remains one of the most aggressive malignancies within the digestive system. Dubbed the king of cancers, it is characterized by challenges in early detection, rapid progression, and a limited array of effective treatment options. While regimens such as AG (nab-paclitaxel plus gemcitabine) and FOLFIRINOX (folinic acid, fluorouracil, irinotecan, and oxaliplatin) have emerged as first-line standards for advanced disease, patients’ outcomes remain exceedingly poor, with median OS less than one year. Furthermore, the efficacy of second-line therapies remains markedly limited, thus emphasizing a significant unmet medical need10,11.

The oncology landscape has been revolutionized in recent years by the rise of immunotherapy. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), including programmed death receptor 1 (PD-1) inhibitors, have demonstrated remarkable efficacy across a spectrum of solid tumors12. However, both NENs and PC exhibit generally low objective response rate (ORR) to ICI monotherapy. Research indicates that their characteristics as “immunologically cold tumors”—such as insufficient immune cell infiltration within the tumor microenvironment, the presence of immunosuppressive cells (M2-type macrophages and regulatory T cells) and an abundance of pro-angiogenic factors are major contributors to this limited therapeutic efficacy13. Mounting data indicates that antiangiogenics and PD-1 inhibitors jointly alter the tumor microenvironment through dual modulation of angiogenesis and antitumor immunity, thereby producing synergistic effects14–16.

Surufatinib, a novel oral small-molecule multi-target inhibitor that potently and simultaneously inhibits vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 1/2/3 (VEGFR1/2/3), fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1), and colony-stimulating factor-1 receptor (CSF-1R)17. It has demonstrated clinical activity in various solid tumors, particularly NENs. Preclinical studies indicate that surufatinib can reduce M2-type tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) while increasing M1-type TAMs18. This immunomodulatory effect may enhance antitumor efficacy when combined with PD-1 inhibitors18. Sintilimab, a monoclonal antibody against PD-1, blocks the interaction between PD-1 and its ligands and helps the antitumor effect of T cells to recover19.

Given the paucity of effective therapies for both high-grade NENs and PC, we explored a combination strategy in these populations. Therefore, this study aims to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of surufatinib combined with sintilimab with or without chemotherapy according to clinical needs, in patients with NEC, NET G3 or PC. The goal is to explore whether this combination regimen could provide new therapeutic opportunities for these populations with extremely poor prognose.

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p:
Between February 2023 and March 2025, a total of 60 patients were screened, and 51 were ultimately enrolled and received treatment. These patients were distributed across three cohorts: 30 in the NEC cohort, 12 in the NET G3 cohort, and 9 in the PC cohort. Patient demographics and baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. In the NEC cohort, the median age was 63 years (range: 45–77), and 73.3% (22/30) of the patients were male. The median Ki-67 index was 80% (range: 60–90%). Notably, 66.7% (20/30) of the patients were receiving first-line treatment. Within the NET G3 cohort, the median age was 54 years (range: 33–76), with 41.7% (5/12) of the patients being male. The median Ki-67 index was 25% (range: 20–40%). sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p:
As of August 31, 2025, the median follow-up time was 18.6 months (95% CI: 15.4–22.8). In the NEC cohort, the median PFS (mPFS) was 7.3 months (95% CI: 6.4–9.3) (Fig. 1A). The median OS (mOS) was 13.3 months (95% CI: 9.3–not evaluable [NE]) (Fig. 1B). The ORR was 53.3% (16/30), and the DCR was 73.3% (22/30) (Fig. 1C–E and Table 2). sec.title: Safety
sec.p:
This study analyzed treatment-related adverse events in 51 patients, as shown in Table 3. The NEC cohort demonstrated more pronounced hematological toxicity: decreased neutrophil count occurred in 93.3% of patients, with 56.6% being grade ≥3; decreased white blood cell count occurred in 86.7%, with 40.0% being grade ≥3. Furthermore, febrile neutropenia occurred in 20.0% of this cohort. In contrast, the NET G3 and PC cohorts receiving dual therapy (surufatinib + sintilimab) showed markedly milder hematological toxicity. The NET G3 cohort primarily exhibited targeted therapy-related adverse events such as proteinuria (75.0%) and hypertension (41.7%), while the PC cohort was characterized by diarrhea (66.6%) and anorexia (44.4%). Regarding gastrointestinal toxicity, nausea occurred in 100.0% of the NEC cohort, with 23.3% being grade ≥3. Meanwhile, the incidence of nausea was significantly lower in the dual-therapy cohorts (33.3% in NET G3 and 22.2% in PC), with no grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse event (TRAE) reported.Table 3

There was no serious adverse event, and no death attributed to TRAE. TRAE caused dose interruption or dose reduction in 17 patients (33.3%), with a frequency of 40.0% (12/30 patients) in the NEC cohort, which was higher than the other 2 cohorts (8.3% for the NET G3 cohort and 11.1% for the PC cohort, respectively).

sec.title: Biomarker analysis
sec.p:
We analyzed bulk RNA sequencing data from ten tumor samples obtained from patients with NEC, including five treatment-sensitive cases (achieving disease remission) and five treatment-resistant cases (with disease progression). Tumor samples were obtained at baseline; no on-treatment or post-progression samples were available. Among the 17,196 detected genes, differential expression genes (DEG) analysis between the two groups identified 50 significantly altered genes, with 22 upregulated in the treatment-sensitive group and 28 upregulated in the treatment-resistant group (Fig. 4A and Fig. S2). We next evaluated the prognostic predictive value of nine selected genes using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Six genes (ARG2, EGLN3, ADM, ESR1, RAB26, and SERPINA3) showed excellent predictive performance with AUC values close to 1.0, while OLFM4, HABP2, and MUC6 also demonstrated remarkably high AUC values of ~0.92, indicating strong prognostic potential (Fig. 4B). Functional enrichment analyses of the differentially expressed genes were performed using Gene Ontology (GO)—including biological processes (BP), cellular components (CC), and molecular functions (MF)—as well as Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis (Fig. 4C). Genes upregulated in the treatment-sensitive group were mainly enriched in pathways associated with heart rate regulation, synaptic membrane components, nutrient binding and biosynthesis, the HIF-1 signaling pathway etc. In contrast, genes upregulated in the treatment-resistant group were enriched in digestion-related processes, vascular and blood–brain barrier transport, hormone activation, etc. Additionally, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that genes upregulated in the sensitive group were closely related to immune-related pathways, including the regulation of BCR/TCR signaling, whereas downregulated genes were enriched in extracellular matrix-related pathways, such as collagen biosynthesis, metalloproteinase activation, and proteoglycan-related processes (Fig. 4D).Fig. 4Transcriptomic landscape defining immunotherapy responsiveness in NEC.
A Differential gene expression analysis comparing responders and non-responders to immunotherapy. Volcano plot highlights significantly altered genes, with 22 upregulated (red) and 28 downregulated (blue) transcripts relative to baseline. B Diagnostic performance of key discriminative genes. ROC curves demonstrate their ability to stratify responders versus non-responders, with AUC reflecting predictive accuracy. C Functional enrichment analysis of response-associated genes. GO (BP, CC, MF) and KEGG pathway analyses identify signaling pathways enriched in responders (left), whereas non-responders show enrichment of secretion function (right). Dot size represents the number of involved genes; color scale indicates adjusted P values. D GSEA of global transcriptional programs. Responders exhibit enrichment of immune-related and antigen-presentation pathways, whereas non-responders display suppression of these signatures. Curves indicate enrichment scores across ranked gene lists. To validate the reliability of these gene signatures, we employed two external datasets GSE142720 and GSE111044, two small-scale transcriptomic profiles of gastroenteropancreatic NEC (n = 7) and esophageal NEC (n = 3) tissues and corresponding normal tissues (n = 3). In addition, transcriptome data from corresponding normal tissues were obtained from the GTEx database for comparison. Two representative genes, EGLN3 and ADM, were significantly upregulated in normal tissues compared with NEC counterparts (Fig. S3A). To further explore the biological functions of these genes, samples were stratified into high- and low-expression groups. To further clarify the oncogenic or tumor-suppressive roles of these DEGs, we analyzed the relationships between gene expression levels and key signaling pathways, including PI3K-Akt, TNF, and cellular senescence pathways (Fig. S3B). Correlation plots based on Spearman’s coefficients revealed that SERPINA3 expression was positively correlated with these pathways, whereas ARG2 showed an opposite trend. Additionally, in the Wnt signaling pathway, MUC6 expression exhibited a positive correlation, while ADM was negatively correlated. Regarding antigen processing and presentation, ADM expression was positively associated, whereas MUC6 showed a negative correlation.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study is an exploratory phase II clinical trial targeting metastatic NEC, NET G3, and PC. It aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of a novel combination strategy involving surufatinib plus sintilimab, with or without chemotherapy. Comparisons with historical controls are descriptive and limited by differences in patient selection, treatment lines, and study design. These data were provided for context but do not establish superiority.

Based on the highly malignant and aggressive biological behavior of NEC, all patients with NEC in this study received chemotherapy. Among first-line treated patients, the ORR was 65.0%, mPFS was 7.6 months, and mOS was 14.3 months, which are significantly higher than previously reported literature data (ORR: 52.5–54.5%, PFS: 5.1–5.6 months, OS: 10.9–12.5 months)20. In second-line treated patients, the ORR was 30.0%, mPFS was 2.3 months, and mOS was 4.8 months, which are comparable to previous literature data (ORR: 10.3–25.0%, PFS: 2.0–3.7 months, OS: 6.0–8.9 months)21–23. In the first-line treatment of metastatic small cell lung cancer, an exploratory study investigating the combination of surufatinib with a PD-1 inhibitor and chemotherapy achieved an unprecedented ORR of 97.1% and a DCR of 100.0%, further validating this treatment approach24. These results indicate that adding surufatinib and immunotherapy to chemotherapy can further enhance efficacy, particularly in first-line treated NEC patients, which may be related to a more active immune cell state in the early stages of the disease.

Tumor angiogenesis can be promoted by various factors, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2), and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF). These pro-angiogenic factors contribute to immunosuppression through multiple complex mechanisms, collectively fostering a microenvironment that permits tumor immune evasion25. Surufatinib potently inhibits both VEGFR1/2/3 and FGFR1, thereby suppressing pathological tumor angiogenesis. Beyond restraining tumor growth, it may also reverse the immunosuppressive microenvironment. Furthermore, by inhibiting CSF-1R, surufatinib modulates TAMs, promoting their polarization from the immunosuppressive M2 phenotype toward the immunostimulatory M1 phenotype. This shift alleviates immunosuppression within the tumor microenvironment and enhances the infiltration and function of effector T cells18. These preclinical insights suggest that dual inhibition of VEGFR and CSF-1R by surufatinib can synergize significantly with PD-1 blockade, resulting in enhanced antitumor efficacy.

Our integrative transcriptomic analysis identified distinct molecular signatures between treatment-sensitive and -resistant NEC samples, highlighting the biological heterogeneity underlying therapeutic outcomes. Notably, genes upregulated in the treatment-sensitive group were functionally enriched in pathways related to cellular metabolism, biosynthesis, and the HIF-1 signaling pathway. These results suggest that metabolic reprogramming and Inhibition of hypoxia-driven responses may contribute to enhanced treatment efficacy26. The previous studies illustrated that under hypoxic conditions, activation of the HIF-1 pathway induces VEGF expression, enhances angiogenesis, and facilitates epithelial cell migration, collectively promoting tumor progression27,28, which may partially account for the enhanced therapeutic response observed in the treatment-sensitive group through regulation of this pathway in our cohort. Conversely, genes overexpressed in the treatment-resistant group were predominantly enriched in digestion-related and vascular transport pathways, implying elevated metabolic demand and microenvironmental remodeling during tumor progression. Such alterations may facilitate nutrient acquisition and drug efflux, thereby contributing to therapeutic resistance. The enrichment of hormone activation and barrier-related processes further indicates potential endocrine and vascular adaptations that may reinforce tumor survival mechanisms.

Among the identified candidate genes, ADM, ARG2, MUC6, and SERPINA3 exhibited particularly strong associations with immune modulation and tumor microenvironmental dynamics. ADM is a 52–amino acid peptide hormone of the calcitonin family that acts through local paracrine and autocrine signaling. Interestingly, its role in cancer prognosis appears context-dependent, being linked to both beneficial and adverse outcomes in different tumor types29. Its high expression was closely associated with enhanced antigen processing and presentation function; this finding suggests that ADM may facilitate more efficient immune recognition and activation of adaptive immune responses, thereby contributing to a more immunostimulatory tumor microenvironment and improved treatment sensitivity. MUC6, a key member of the mucin family, is predominantly expressed in gastrointestinal epithelial cells, where it helps maintain epithelial integrity. By contributing to the protection and remodeling of the epithelial barrier, MUC6 provides a supportive environment for epithelial cell migration and cancer progression30; its association with cellular senescence signatures suggests a tumor-promoting and immunosuppressive role. Similarly, ARG2 appeared to mitigate immune exhaustion, consistent with reports that arginine metabolism modulates T-cell function and antitumor responses31. SERPINA3, which showed positive correlations with PI3K-Akt, TNF signaling and cellular senescence pathways, may participate in pro-tumorigenic signaling and inflammatory regulation, emphasizing its multifaceted contribution to tumor progression. Consistent with previous studies, SERPINA3 has been implicated in several oncogenic processes, such as promoting invasion and metastasis, enhancing angiogenesis, and facilitating the evasion of growth suppressors32–34. Together, these findings underscore the complex interplay between metabolic adaptation, immune modulation, and tumor microenvironmental remodeling in determining therapeutic response. The identification of key regulators such as ADM, MUC6, ARG2, and SERPINA3 not only provides insights into the biological mechanisms driving treatment sensitivity and resistance but also offers potential targets for therapeutic intervention. Genes with high AUC values are potential candidates but require validation in larger cohorts. Further mechanistic and clinical validation studies are warranted to explore their utility.

There is currently no established standard for first- or second-line treatment of metastatic NET G3. Management generally follows a strategy similar to that for NET G1/G2, incorporating CAPTEM chemotherapy, targeted agents, and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT)35. In a large prospective observational study36, most of the NET G3 patients (117/128) received first-line chemotherapy. Of these, 39% were treated with platinum-based regimens plus etoposide, 57% received temozolomide-based therapy. However, outcomes with platinum-etoposide were notably poor in NET G3 compared with other regimens, which was distinctly different from patients with NEC. The ORR was 28% with a median PFS of 7.4 months. PD was observed in 21% of patients at the first radiological assessment, underscoring the generally poor outcomes in this population. In our study, which included NET G3 patients across various treatment lines, the ORR was 16.7%, and mPFS was 6.8 months. The combination of targeted therapy and immunotherapy remains a promising approach worthy of further exploration in NET G3 patients.

PC has long been known as an “immune desert”, with single-agent ICI demonstrating minimal efficacy (ORR <5%)37. In the PC cohort of this study, an ORR of 22.2%, a mPFS of 2.1 months, and a mOS of 5.5 months were observed, preliminarily indicating the potential efficacy of the combination therapy strategies. Previous studies have shown that chemotherapy with the AG regimen could induce an increase in M2-type TAMs and upregulation of CSF-1R, contributing to an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, surufatinib has been demonstrated to reverse this process and synergize with PD-1 antibodies to activate CD8 + T-cell function38,39. This mechanism provides a novel strategic approach for combination immunotherapy in pancreatic cancer and warrants further clinical translation and exploration.

All patients in our study received surufatinib combined with sintilimab, with the NEC cohort additionally receiving chemotherapy. Thus, efficacy in NEC cannot be attributed solely to the combination; chemotherapy likely contributes substantially. The addition of chemotherapy significantly enhanced hematological toxicity, particularly the risk of neutropenia and febrile neutropenia. The dual therapy regimen of surufatinib combined with sintilimab primarily manifested typical targeted therapy-related adverse events such as proteinuria and hypertension, which were consistent with previous findings40,41. These findings suggest that tailored adverse event prevention and management strategies should be developed according to the specific treatment regimen. For patients receiving surufatinib, intensified monitoring of blood pressure and urinary protein is recommended; for patients receiving chemotherapy, routine use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor for primary prevention of hematological toxicity is advised.

This study has several limitations. First, as a single-center, phase II trial, its sample size is relatively limited, and the absence of a randomized control group may introduce selection bias. Subgroup analyses are also limited by small numbers of patients, precluding robust statistical inference. Second, although the addition of chemotherapy was determined by the investigators, which reflects real-world clinical practice, this inevitably introduced heterogeneity, which may have influenced the efficacy outcomes. Further validation through larger sample, randomized controlled studies is needed to confirm the conclusions of this trial.

This is an exploratory, hypothesis-generating study evaluating a biologically plausible combination in three distinct malignancies. Results are presented pooled for efficiency but interpreted with caution due to inter-tumor heterogeneity. Definitive conclusions require validation in disease-specific trials. We also clarified that dual therapy (surufatinib + sintilimab) was used in NET G3/ PC, while triplet therapy (adding chemotherapy) was used in NEC, acknowledging this as a key source of heterogeneity.

The combination of surufatinib and sintilimab showed preliminary efficacy and a manageable safety profile in patients with NEC, NET G3, and PC, but efficacy in NEC is confounded by chemotherapy. Findings are exploratory, and confirmatory studies in the future are highly anticipated.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: This prospective phase II clinical trial was designed as a multiple-arm, single-center study conducted at the Department of Gastrointestinal Oncology, Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute and Hospital. The study enrolled patients aged 18 to 75 years with histologically confirmed inoperable or recurrent NEC, NET G3 or PC. Pathological diagnosis was made locally per WHO criteria. Central pathology review was not performed due to resource constraints, which is a limitation. Cases were reviewed by two experienced pathologists at our center to minimize misclassification. Eligible NEC and NET G3 patients included those who had experienced disease progression or intolerance to prior standard therapy, as well as those who had not received any systematic treatment. For PC patients, progression after prior standard therapy was required. Additional key inclusion criteria comprised an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status (ECOG PS) score of 0 or 1, at least one measurable lesion based on RECIST 1.1 criteria, and adequate bone marrow reserve and organ function.

Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute and Hospital (number E20200562), aligned with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice. All patients provided a written informed consent form before enrollment. This study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov with registration number NCT05627427.

sec.title: Treatment and assessment
sec.p: All enrolled patients received the following combination regimen. Surufatinib: 250 mg (administered as five 50 mg capsules), taken orally once daily after breakfast. Sintilimab: 200 mg, administered via intravenous infusion every three weeks. NEC patients received platinum-etoposide or irinotecan-based hemotherapy, administered every 3 weeks for four to six cycles. Regimens were determined by the investigators based on each patient’s prior treatment history, overall clinical condition, and prevailing medical practice.

Treatment was continued until disease progression (as defined by RECIST 1.1), occurrence of intolerable toxicity, withdrawal of informed consent, or study termination. Tumor response was assessed according to RECIST 1.1 using contrast-enhanced CT or MRI. Imaging evaluations were performed at baseline, every two cycles during treatment, and every three months after treatment completion. Survival follow-up was conducted every three months for up to 24 months or until death. Safety was evaluated according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (NCI-CTCAE) version 5.0, with assessments performed at baseline, at the end of each treatment cycle, and until 90 days after treatment discontinuation. Additionally, baseline tumor tissue samples from selected patients underwent RNA sequencing to characterize the impact of combination therapy on the tumor and immune microenvironment.

The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS), which was defined as the duration from the initiation of study treatment to the earliest instance of progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first. The secondary study endpoints were designated as the ORR, disease control rate (DCR), OS and safety. PFS was chosen as the primary endpoint to capture early antitumor activity, align with FDA guidance for advanced NENs, and account for the aggressive nature of NEC/PC (where OS may be truncated by rapid progression). ORR was determined by the proportion of patients achieving a confirmed complete response (CR) and partial remission (PR) based on RECIST 1.1 criteria. DCR was defined as the proportion of patients who showed a CR, PR, or stable disease (SD) state per the RECIST 1.1 criteria. OS was measured from the initiation of study treatment to death from any cause. Safety evaluations were graded using the common toxicity criteria outlined in the NCI-CTCAE V5.0.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: As an exploratory phase II study, no formal sample size calculation was performed. Sample size was based on feasibility and prior phase II trials in similar populations. The statistical analysis was performed utilizing SAS 9.4 software. The Kaplan–Meier method was used to estimate the PFS and OS. Survival comparison between groups utilized the log-rank test, and the Cox proportional hazard model facilitated between-group analyses for the PFS and OS, along with estimating the corresponding 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). The median follow-up time for survival was calculated with the reverse Kaplan–Meier method. The Clopper–Pearson method was also used to assess the 95% CI for the ORR and DCR, with differences evaluated using Chi-squared or Fisher’s exact tests. The significance level was set at α = 0.05 (two-sided). Safety data were analyzed using descriptive statistical methods.

sec.title: Ethics and consent
sec.p: Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute and Hospital (reference number: E20200562), aligned with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice. All patients provided written informed consent before enrollment. This study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov with registration number NCT05627427 on November 15, 2022.
